```{=html}
<header class="dg-head dg-head-section"><p class="dg-kicker">Appendix B <span class="dg-sep">•</span> <a href="index.html">Proofs &amp; Comments</a></p><h1 class="dg-title"><span class="dg-secnum">B.2</span> Hamel and Schauder Bases (§<a class="dg-xref" href="../vector-spaces/basis-components-transformations.html" data-kind="section" data-label="section_Basis_Components_Transformations">2.3</a>)</h1></header>
<p>This appendix expands on the brief comment made in Section <a class="dg-xref" href="../vector-spaces/basis-components-transformations.html" data-kind="section" data-label="section_Basis_Components_Transformations">2.3</a> regarding the nature of bases in vector spaces. Specifically, it clarifies the distinction between <strong>Hamel bases</strong>, which rely on finite linear combinations, and <strong>Schauder bases</strong>, which involve infinite sums defined only when a compatible topology is present.</p>
<div class="dg-skip dg-medskip"></div>
<p>The concept of a <strong>basis</strong> in linear algebra—formally called a <strong>Hamel basis</strong>—requires that every vector in the space can be expressed as a <strong>finite</strong> linear combination of elements from the basis. This finite expansion is fundamental to the definition of a basis in the context of pure vector spaces. Specifically, the decomposition <span class="math display">\[
    \mathcal{X} = (x^1 \cdot \hat{x}_1) \oplus \dots \oplus (x^d \cdot \hat{x}_d)
\]</span> must always involve only finitely many terms for any vector <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{X} \in V\)</span>.</p>
<div class="dg-skip dg-medskip"></div>
<p>If we were to drop the requirement that only finite sums are allowed in the decomposition, the expression for a vector would become an <strong>infinite sum</strong>, i.e., an <strong>infinite series</strong>. However, the concept of summing infinitely many vectors is not meaningful in the context of pure vector spaces alone, since the axioms of vector spaces do not include any notion of <em>limit</em>, <em>convergence</em>, or <em>closeness</em>.</p>
<div class="dg-skip dg-medskip"></div>
<p>To give meaning to such infinite sums, the vector space must be equipped with additional structure, specifically, a <strong>topology</strong> compatible with the vector space operations. This leads to the concept of a <strong>topological vector space</strong>, and in particular, to the notion of a <strong>Schauder basis</strong> (also called a <strong>topological basis</strong>). A Schauder basis allows vectors to be expressed as (potentially) infinite sums that converge in the topology of the space.</p>
<div class="dg-skip dg-medskip"></div>
<p>The distinction between Hamel and Schauder bases has profound consequences:</p>
<ul class="dg-itemize dg-depth-1">
<li><p>In <strong>finite-dimensional vector spaces</strong>, the two notions coincide trivially, since infinite sums do not arise.</p></li>
<li><p>In <strong>infinite-dimensional vector spaces</strong>, a Hamel basis always exists (assuming the Axiom of Choice), but it is almost never useful in practice. Hamel bases for function spaces like <span class="math inline">\(L^2([0,1])\)</span>—the set of all square-integrable functions on the interval <span class="math inline">\([0,1]\)</span>—are uncountably infinite, highly pathological, and bear no relation to the orthonormal bases commonly used in analysis (such as Fourier bases), which are Schauder bases.</p></li>
<li><p>Conversely, Schauder bases are <strong>countable</strong> (when they exist) and tied to the topology of the space. These bases enable the powerful machinery of infinite series and convergence, which is essential for functional analysis, partial differential equations, and quantum mechanics.</p></li>
</ul>
<div class="dg-skip dg-medskip"></div>
<p>In summary, the restriction to <strong>finite sums</strong> in the definition of a Hamel basis is not an arbitrary technicality but a fundamental reflection of the fact that pure vector spaces, as defined in algebra, do not possess any notion of convergence or topology.</p>
```
